title: How Long Does an HVAC System Last?
h1: How Long Does an HVAC System Last in a Southern California Home?
description: Most AC units and heat pumps last about 10 to 15 years and furnaces often run longer. Learn what shortens HVAC lifespan and the signs it's time to replace.
quick_answer: Most central air conditioners and heat pumps last roughly 10 to 15 years, and gas furnaces often last 15 to 20 years or more. Real lifespan depends on how well the system was sized and installed, how hard it works, how close it sits to the ocean and how consistently it gets maintenance.
body:
Those ranges are general, and plenty of systems fall outside them in either direction. We've seen furnaces that are still going strong after decades and air conditioners that wore out early because they were oversized, undercharged or never serviced. Here's what makes the difference.

How long does each part of the system usually last?

An "HVAC system" is really several pieces of equipment, and they don't all age at the same rate.

  • Central air conditioner: roughly 10 to 15 years. The outdoor unit takes the most abuse from sun, salt air and heat.
  • Heat pump: roughly 10 to 15 years. It runs in both summer and winter, so it often logs more hours than an AC.
  • Gas furnace: often 15 to 20 years or more. In mild coastal areas a furnace may run so little that age catches up with it before wear does.
  • Ductless mini-split: often similar to a heat pump when it's kept clean and serviced.
  • Ductwork: metal duct can last for decades. Older flex duct in a hot attic can sag, tear or come loose much sooner.
  • Thermostat: usually replaced for features long before it fails.

What shortens the life of an HVAC system in San Diego and Orange County?

Our climate is easy on equipment in some ways and hard on it in others.

  • Salt air. Homes near the coast see faster corrosion on outdoor coils, fins and electrical parts.
  • Inland heat. Systems in hotter inland neighborhoods run long cycles all summer, which adds wear to compressors and fan motors.
  • Attic installs. Furnaces and air handlers in attics bake through the summer, which is tough on wiring, control boards and duct connections.
  • Dirty filters. A clogged filter starves the system of airflow, makes it run hotter and longer, and can freeze an AC coil.
  • Wrong sizing. An oversized unit short-cycles, turning on and off constantly. An undersized one never gets a break.
  • Skipped maintenance. Small problems like a weak capacitor or low refrigerant turn into big repairs when nobody catches them.

What are the signs an HVAC system is near the end?

Age alone isn't a reason to replace equipment that's still running well. Look for a combination of these:

  • Repairs are getting more frequent, or a single repair would be a big share of the cost of new equipment
  • Some rooms are always too hot or too cold, even after adjustments
  • Energy bills keep creeping up without a change in how you use the system
  • The system is noisy, smells burnt or musty, or cycles on and off constantly
  • The AC uses R-22 refrigerant, which is no longer produced, so recharging it is costly
  • A furnace has a cracked heat exchanger or keeps tripping its safety switches

If you smell gas, leave the house and call your gas utility from outside. If a carbon monoxide alarm goes off, get everyone out and call 911.

How can you make your system last longer?

Most of what extends equipment life is simple and routine:

  1. Change or clean the filter on schedule, more often during wildfire smoke or if you have pets.
  2. Keep plants, fences and trash bins a couple of feet away from the outdoor unit.
  3. Rinse salt and dust off the outdoor coil with a gentle hose spray, with the power off.
  4. Book a tune-up once a year, or twice a year for a heat pump that heats and cools.
  5. Fix duct leaks and disconnected runs so the system isn't working harder than it should.

Should you repair or replace an older system?

If the system is under ten years old and the repair is modest, repairing usually makes sense. Once equipment is in the back half of its expected life and needs a major part like a compressor or heat exchanger, it's often smarter to put that money toward a new, more efficient system. A good technician will give you both options and let you decide.

If you're weighing that decision, our HVAC repair and replacement team can inspect the system, tell you honestly how much life is left and give you a free estimate on either path.
faqs: Does a furnace last longer in San Diego than in colder places?

Often, yes. Mild winters mean fewer heating hours, especially near the coast. But furnaces in hot attics still age from heat exposure, and a furnace that sits unused for months should still be inspected before the first cold night.

Usually not for a major repair. Most 20-year-old AC units are well past their expected life, less efficient than current equipment and may use R-22 refrigerant. A small fix can buy time, but it's a good moment to start planning a replacement.
How often should my HVAC system be serviced?
Once a year is a good baseline for most homes. Heat pumps that handle both heating and cooling benefit from a check in spring and fall. Filters should be checked monthly and changed as needed.
